exam: A 25‑year‑old with tendon xanthomas and a family history of early MI – what is the most likely diagnosis and why is genetic testing useful? — Familial hypercholesterolaemia; LDL‑R mutation confirms diagnosis and guides cascade screening.

A patient with HIV on protease inhibitors presents with elevated LDL‑C – how does the drug cause this change and what is the first-line lipid‑lowering strategy? — Protease inhibitors up‑regulate hepatic VLDL synthesis; start a statin (preferably pravastatin) after checking liver function.

In a rural clinic without lipid panels, a patient has premature coronary disease – how would you assess and manage dyslipidaemia? — Use clinical risk scores, look for xanthomas, start lifestyle measures, and consider empiric statin if no contraindications.

A child with recurrent pancreatitis has triglycerides of 800 mg/dL – what is the underlying metabolic problem and immediate management? — Hypertriglyceridaemia; initiate fasting, IV fluids, and consider fibrate therapy once labs are available.

How does cholestasis affect cholesterol levels and what clinical clues help you identify it? — Impaired bile‑acid excretion reduces cholesterol clearance, leading to hypercholesterolaemia; look for jaundice, pruritus, and raised ALP.
Why is measuring LDL‑C alone insufficient in patients with HIV on antiretroviral therapy? — ART also raises triglycerides and lowers HDL‑C, both contributing to risk; a full lipid profile is needed.

A patient on rifampicin shows low cholesterol – what is the mechanism and does it require treatment? — Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes accelerating cholesterol synthesis and clearance; usually no treatment needed unless symptomatic.
What are the contraindications for statin use in low‑resource settings? — Active liver disease, pregnancy, severe renal impairment; avoid if baseline transaminases >3× upper limit.
ai.title: Cholesterol Metabolism
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Cholesterol is converted to steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D. Understanding its pathways helps diagnose dyslipidaemia, liver disease, and endocrine disorders, especially where tests are limited.

b: Endogenous synthesis accounts for ~80% of body cholesterol.
Key organ: liver – site of synthesis, conversion, and clearance.
sections.p: Cholesterol is a lipid essential for cell membranes, hormone synthesis, bile acid formation, and vitamin D production. In low‑resource settings, disturbances often present as premature cardiovascular disease or liver dysfunction.

The mevalonate pathway starts with acetyl‑CoA, forming HMG‑CoA, then mevalonate via HMG‑CoA reductase (rate‑limiting step). Mevalonate is converted to isoprenoids, then to squalene and finally cholesterol. Cholesterol is conjugated to bile acids or used for steroid hormones.

b: High cellular cholesterol ↓ HMG‑CoA reductase activity.
sections.p: Feedback inhibition by intracellular cholesterol, LDL‑receptor mediated uptake, and hormonal control (insulin up‑regulates, glucagon down‑regulates). Inflammation and infections (e.g., HIV, TB) can alter lipid profiles.

b: Genetic LDL‑R or APOB loss → high LDL‑C, early MI.
HIV protease inhibitors ↑ VLDL and LDL‑C.
TB treatment (rifampicin) induces hepatic enzymes, lowering cholesterol.
Schistosomiasis can cause cholestasis, raising bilirubin and cholesterol.
sections.p: Disorders include familial hypercholesterolaemia, secondary dyslipidaemia (malaria, HIV, hepatitis B), and cholestatic liver disease. Severe hypercholesterolaemia accelerates atherosclerosis; impaired bile‑acid synthesis causes fat malabsorption.

b: Elevated alkaline phosphatase with jaundice → cholestasis affecting cholesterol clearance.
sections.p: Patients may present with premature coronary artery disease, xanthomas, or fat‑soluble vitamin deficiency. In low‑resource hospitals, lipid panels may be unavailable; clinicians rely on clinical clues and basic liver function tests.

t.b: Is the patient hyperlipidaemic? High LDL‑C (>130 mg/dL) supports dyslipidaemia; normal values make other causes more likely.
Is cholestasis present? Raised ALP and bilirubin suggest impaired bile‑acid synthesis, affecting cholesterol clearance.
Are glucose and renal function adequate for statin use? If unavailable, assess clinically for diabetes or renal disease before prescribing.

b: Remember HMG‑CoA reductase is the rate‑limiting enzyme.
LDL‑R up‑regulation occurs when cellular cholesterol is low.
In HIV, protease inhibitors raise LDL‑C and triglycerides.
sections.p: Focus on pathway steps, regulation, and common secondary causes in the tropics. Be ready to differentiate primary genetic dyslipidaemia from infection‑related lipid changes and to outline management without full lipid panels.
